deckTitle: Multi-Tenant Agentic AI on Google Cloud: Reference Taxonomy & 5-Hop Governance (Workstream 1)
deckSubtitle: Official Google Cloud Architecture Center hub-and-spoke reference architecture comparing Pooled (Pattern A), Sovereign Silos (Pattern B), and Dynamic Hybrid (Pattern C) isolation models
tldr: The Multi-Tenant Agentic Challenge: Provisioning dedicated cloud projects for Standard Tiernth commercial tenants erodes SaaS gross margins, whereas naive shared runtimes expose cross-tenant tool, memory, and quota surfaces.

Four Agentic Threat Vectors: Unlike deterministic CRUD applications, autonomous ADK agents dynamically discover MCP tools, persist episodic Memory Bank state, share prompt caches, and consume variable reasoning tokens.

Three Production Isolation Topologies: Pattern A (High-Density Pooled), Pattern B (Zero-Trust Sovereign Silos), and Pattern C (Dynamic Hybrid PSC Spokes) reuse 80% of the same Python ADK 2.0 application codebase.

Five-Hop Cryptographic Defense-in-Depth: Every agent turn enforces verified tenant context across Edge OBO/DPoP (Hop 1), Registry Discovery (Hop 2), Memory & Quotas (Hop 3), Model Armor/SDP (Hop 4), and AlloyDB RLS (Hop 5).

Architecture Center & CISO Deliverable Kit: Ships with the Google Cloud Architecture Center (#78) hub-and-spoke blueprint, 20 automated red-team/migration assertions, and production compensating controls for EAP product gaps.

sections.heading: Products used — Google Cloud Agentic AI, Security & Data Stack
bullets: Agentic AI & Foundation Models: Vertex AI Agent Engine (ADK 2.0 runtime, Agent Registry & L1–L5 Memory Bank), Gemini 2.5 Pro with ContextCacheConfig (90% shared prefix discount), Vertex AI Model Garden (Gemini 2.5 Pro (Dedicated PT)), and Gemma 3 (27B) on private GKE.

Ingress, Identity & AI Safety Guardrails: Global External Application Load Balancer, Google Cloud Armor L7 WAF, Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) & IAM Security Token Service (RFC 8693 OBO + RFC 9449 DPoP), Vertex AI Model Armor, and Cloud Sensitive Data Protection (DLP).

Data, Storage, Networking & Governance: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL (FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY), Memorystore for Valkey (per-tenant RPM bulkheads) & Firestore, VPC Service Controls (VPC-SC) & Private Service Connect (PSC), Cloud KMS CMEK (HTTP 423 kill-switch), and BigQuery OTel.

Shared 80% Reusable Application Core: All three isolation patterns execute the exact same Python ADK 2.0 5-hop security pipeline (`core-cymbal-agent/runtime_pipeline.py`), parameterizing only the surrounding 20% Google Cloud project and network boundary.

FinVault Bank (Regulated Enterprise Tenant): Authenticates via Google Workspace OIDC, provisions a private Gemini 2.5 Pro (Dedicated PT) / Gemma 3 27B regulatory agent (Agent Alpha), receives a 600 RPM / 8,000-token thinking budget, and mandates VPC-SC & Cloud KMS CMEK.

sections.heading: Design alternatives — Compensating Controls for EAP Product Gaps (GAP-01..05)
tableRows:
GAP-01 (Hop 2)
Agent Engine Registry
Shared Agent Engine Registry lacks native per-tenant IAM condition predicates on `ListAgents` discovery calls.
`Hop2AgentRegistryDiscovery.filter_ard_catalog` validates signed JWT `tenant_id` against visibility metadata before LLM tool binding.
WS2 Test 2 PASS (`HTTP 403` on cross-tenant Agent Alpha discovery) • Target GA: Q4 2026

GAP-02 (Hop 3)
Memory Bank CMEK
Pooled Vertex AI Memory Bank supports project-level CMEK rather than distinct per-tenant KMS keys in one shared pool.
Pattern A applies envelope encryption via tenant KMS keys; Pattern B isolates each tenant in a dedicated CMEK project (`HTTP 423`).
WS3 Tests 4A/4B/6 PASS (`HTTP 423 Locked` <60s on key disable) • Target GA: Q4 2026

GAP-03 (Hop 3)
Per-Tenant Rate Quotas
Vertex AI quota system enforces regional project-level RPM/TPM limits rather than native per-tenant sub-quotas.
`Hop3RuntimeAndMemory` enforces atomic per-tenant token-bucket RPM limits in Memorystore for Valkey (`120` vs. `600` RPM) + `thinking_budget` clamps.
WS2 Test 6 PASS (`HTTP 429` on 500-RPM flood; budget clamped to 4k) • Target GA: Q4 2026

GAP-04 (Hop 1/2)
Multi-IdP 3LO Broker
External Microsoft Entra ID OIDC tokens require custom claims normalization and step-up consent for downstream MCP tools.
Hop 1 Edge STS normalizes Entra ID `tid`/`sub` claims into DPoP-bound `TenantSecurityContext` with `-32042` step-up 3LO elicitation.
WS2 Test 10 PASS (`HTTP 401` step-up challenge -> `200 OK` ServiceNow) • Target GA: Q4 2026

GAP-05 (Hop 5)
Zero-PII Token Billing
Cloud Billing exports aggregate Vertex AI SKU charges by GCP project rather than individual logical SaaS `tenant_id`.
`Hop5DataAndFinOps` emits zero-PII OpenTelemetry spans (`cached_tokens`, `thinking_tokens`, `output_tokens`) to BigQuery chargeback ledger.
Forensic Check F-08 PASS (3 billing SQL models verified in BigQuery) • Target GA: Q1 2027

sections.heading: Design considerations — 5-Hop Cryptographic Verification Pipeline

pipelineSteps.title: Perimeter WAF, Federated OIDC & DPoP Token Binding
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Strips unauthenticated X-Tenant-Id headers at the L7 load balancer, verifies Google Workspace or Microsoft Entra ID OIDC JWTs, and exchanges credentials via RFC 8693 OBO.
pipelineSteps.invariant: Cryptographic Claim: tenant_id + tier + DPoP (RFC 9449 jkt)
pipelineSteps.gate: HTTP 401 on Spoofed Header or Replayed Bearer Token

pipelineSteps.title: Tenant-Scoped Agent & MCP Tool Catalog Filtering
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Evaluates the signed TenantSecurityContext against Agent Engine Registry metadata before LLM tool-binding, returning only shared platform tools and tenant-owned private agents.
pipelineSteps.gate: HTTP 403 Forbidden on Cross-Tenant Agent or MCP Discovery

pipelineSteps.title: Sandboxed ADK 2.0 Execution, L1–L5 Memory & Quota Bulkheads
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Executes agent reasoning inside gVisor-isolated Cloud Run v2 / Agent Engine sandboxes, partitions L1–L5 Memory Bank namespaces, and enforces per-tenant RPM and thinking budgets.
pipelineSteps.gate: HTTP 429 on RPM Burst • HTTP 403 on Cross-Namespace Read

pipelineSteps.title: Bidirectional Model Armor Screening & Sensitive Data Redaction
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Screens ingress prompts and retrieved RAG chunks for prompt injection/jailbreaks, enforces tenant Natural Language Constraints (NLCs), and redacts egress PII/PCI/IBAN tokens.
pipelineSteps.invariant: Policy: inspectContent + deidentifyContent + Tenant NLC Rules
pipelineSteps.gate: HTTP 400 on Prompt Injection • HTTP 422 on NLC Policy Breach

pipelineSteps.title: Transactional Row-Level Security, CMEK & Zero-PII Telemetry
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Binds parameterized PostgreSQL session context (app.current_tenant_id) for mandatory Row-Level Security, verifies Cloud KMS CMEK liveness, and streams zero-PII OTel spans to BigQuery.
pipelineSteps.invariant: SQL: SET LOCAL app.current_tenant_id • OTel Chargeback Ledger
pipelineSteps.gate: 0 Unauthorized Rows • HTTP 423 Locked on CMEK Revocation

bullets: Hop 1 — Edge WAF & Identity Binding: Cloud Armor strips spoofed X-Tenant-Id headers while IAP and IAM STS mint an RFC 8693 OBO + RFC 9449 DPoP TenantSecurityContext.
Hop 2 — Registry Discovery Filtering: Vertex AI Agent Engine Registry evaluates tenant visibility metadata prior to tool binding, returning HTTP 403 on unauthorized private agents.
Hop 3 — Sandboxed Runtime & Quota Bulkheads: Cloud Run v2 and Memorystore for Valkey isolate L1–L5 Memory Bank namespaces and clamp per-tenant RPM (120/600) and thinking budgets (4k/8k).
Hop 4 — Bidirectional Model Armor & DLP: Model Armor blocks prompt injection (HTTP 400) and semantic NLC violations (HTTP 422), while Sensitive Data Protection masks IBAN/SWIFT/PAN tokens.
Hop 5 — Transactional RLS, CMEK & FinOps: AlloyDB enforces SET LOCAL app.current_tenant_id Row-Level Security, Cloud KMS validates CMEK liveness (HTTP 423), and BigQuery logs zero-PII OTel spans.

sections.heading: Design considerations — Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework Alignment
bullets: 1. Security, Privacy & Compliance: Enforces zero-trust defense-in-depth across all 5 hops—combining RFC 9449 DPoP sender-constrained tokens, Model Armor prompt/egress screening, AlloyDB RLS, and revocable Cloud KMS CMEK.

2. Reliability & Fault Isolation: Prevents noisy-neighbor cascading failures through Memorystore for Valkey token-bucket bulkheads, gVisor execution sandboxes, and zero-downtime 3-phase live tier migrations (`0` dropped sessions).

3. Cost Optimization (FinOps): Shares a 32,000-token immutable system prefix in Gemini 2.5 Pro ContextCacheConfig (90% discount, 84.7% net token savings) and streams per-tenant OTel token spans to BigQuery.

4. Operational Excellence & 5. Performance Optimization: Reuses 80% of the Python ADK 2.0 codebase across all 3 patterns, validates 20/20 security simulations in CI/CD, and bounds p99 latency via per-tier thinking budgets (4k vs. 8k).

diagrams.title: Vertex AI Agent Engine Multi-Tenant Taxonomy: Pooled (A), Sovereign Silos (B) & Hybrid (C)
talkingPoints: Step 1 & 2 (Zone 1 Routing Hub): Global ALB, Cloud Armor WAF, and IAP authenticate tenant callers, strip spoofed headers, and look up the tenant isolation pattern.
Zone 2 (Central Governance Hub): Security Command Center, Cloud KMS CMEK, and BigQuery OTel centralize threat detection, key lifecycle, and zero-PII chargeback.
Step 3 Tier Dispatch: The 80% reusable ADK control plane routes requests dynamically to Pattern A (Yellow Spoke) or Pattern B/C (Red Spoke).
Zone 3 (Pattern A Pooled Spoke): Enforces Model Armor screening (4/6), Gemini 2.5 Pro 90% prefix caching (5), Valkey RPM bulkheads, and AlloyDB RLS.
Zone 4 (Pattern B Silos & Pattern C PSC Spoke): Enforces VPC-SC perimeters, IAM PAB, air-gapped Gemma 3 / Gemini 2.5 Pro endpoints, and tenant CMEK kill-switches.

diagrams.title: Google Cloud Architecture Center (#78): Multi-Tenant Agentic AI with 5-Hop Governance
talkingPoints: Extends the canonical Google Cloud Architecture Center hub-and-spoke diagram with 5 mandatory cryptographic tenant isolation hops.
Zone 1 (Hops 1 & 2): Cloud Armor, IAP OBO/DPoP, and Agent Engine Registry authenticate callers and filter the tool catalog before model invocation.
Zone 2 (Hop 5 FinOps & Security): 2LO/3LO Auth Broker, Security Command Center, and BigQuery OTel govern external credentials and per-tenant token attribution.
Zone 3 (FinVault Enterprise Workload): Executes with an 8,000-token thinking budget, OCC semantic NLCs, IBAN/SWIFT SDP masking, and Google Workspace/Jira 3LO.
Zone 4 (RetailStream Standard Workload): Executes with a 4,000-token thinking cap, PCI-DSS PAN masking, Entra ID/ServiceNow 3LO, and AlloyDB RLS.

takeaways: Enforce Cryptographic Context Across All 5 Hops: Database row filters alone cannot secure agentic AI; tenant identity must govern ingress, tool discovery, memory namespaces, safety guardrails, and SQL RLS.

Align Isolation Topology to Regulatory & Margin Requirements: Deploy Pattern A (120 RPM Pool) for commercial scale, Pattern B (600 RPM Silo) for regulated sovereignty, and Pattern C for multi-tier SaaS portfolios.
Maintain a Single 80% Reusable Agent Codebase: Parameterize isolation boundaries via declarative Firestore profiles and Terraform modules rather than forking separate application codebases.

Capture 90% Prefix Cache Savings Without Cross-Tenant Risk: Bind Gemini 2.5 Pro ContextCacheConfig strictly to immutable platform instructions while isolating tenant episodic state in L1–L5 Memory Bank.
Validate Every Release Against Automated Red-Team Gates: Execute the 20-assertion verification suite (10 Pattern A breach tests, 6 Pattern B silo tests, 4 Pattern C migration tests) in CI/CD.

slideSpeakerNotes.fullText:
Welcome everyone. Whether you are looking at this platform from an executive business perspective, a product strategy lens, or hands-on cloud architecture, we have structured this twelve-slide briefing into three clear acts so you always know where we are in the story.

In this session, we are walking through our foundational architecture for running multi-tenant AI agents on Google Cloud—showing how one platform can safely serve both high-volume commercial customers and strictly regulated enterprises without compromising margins or security.

With that three-act roadmap in mind, let's turn to Slide 2 to meet the actual customer profiles whose business and regulatory requirements drive every design decision in this architecture.

slideSpeakerNotes.title: Act I — Customer Use Cases, Competing Tenant Profiles & Cloud Stack
slideSpeakerNotes.whyHere: Following our opening roadmap on Slide 1, we always start with the customer first—because an architecture only creates business value when it solves real customer constraints.
slideSpeakerNotes.whatIsHappening: Here you can see the core business tension every enterprise AI platform faces, illustrated through two very different customers on our Cymbal platform. On one side, FinVault Bank is a regulated financial institution that demands dedicated reasoning capacity, strict compliance guardrails, and customer-controlled encryption keys. On the other side, RetailStream Corp is a fast-moving enterprise retailer running on Microsoft Entra and ServiceNow that needs instant onboarding and predictable unit costs. For our business leaders, we want one unified product offering for both; for our technical and security leaders, we need an absolute guarantee that their data, tools, and performance will never cross company boundaries.
slideSpeakerNotes.whatComesNext: Now that we see what our customers require on Slide 2, the natural question for both business and technical leaders is: what are our architectural options to deliver this, and how do we choose the right one? Let's look at Slide 3.

slideSpeakerNotes.title: Act II (Level 1 Zoom) — 3-Zone Logical Security & Trust Boundary
slideSpeakerNotes.whyHere: Now that we have chosen our architectural approach on Slide 3, Slide 4 opens Act II at Level 1 of our top-down zoom—giving everyone a simple three-zone mental map before we look at the full physical schematic.
slideSpeakerNotes.whatIsHappening: Think of this high-level diagram like the floor plan of a secure airport terminal. Before we look at individual cloud services, everything in our platform is organized into three clear trust zones from left to right. Zone 1 on the left is our Front Door, where customer identity is verified and untrusted traffic is screened. Zone 2 in the center is our Five-Hop Security and Agent Control Plane, which stamps every request with a verified tenant passport and enforces per-customer quotas. Zone 3 on the right contains the isolated execution lanes where the AI models, tools, and databases actually run.

slideSpeakerNotes.title: Act III — Deterministic Fail-Closed Circuit Breakers & Recovery Loop
slideSpeakerNotes.whyHere: On the previous slide, we saw how a normal customer request is verified and sealed at the wire level. As we move into Act III, the natural question from any executive, risk officer, or architect is: what happens during an emergency—whether that is a sudden traffic spike from a noisy neighbor, a policy violation, or a customer revoking their encryption key?
slideSpeakerNotes.whatIsHappening: What you are looking at here is our fail-closed safety circuit. Unlike brittle systems that fail open or hang when a downstream service is overloaded, every gate in our five-hop pipeline acts as an automatic circuit breaker. At the front door, replayed tokens or unauthorized cross-tenant tool calls are rejected immediately. In the middle, our rate-limit bulkhead caps any single tenant that exceeds their requests-per-minute or thinking-token budget so one busy customer never slows down or drives up costs for anyone else. And at the data layer, if an enterprise customer flips their Cloud KMS encryption kill-switch, our system flushes their active memory cache within sixty seconds and locks data access—then automatically re-hydrates from AlloyDB as soon as their security team restores the key.
